I shipped coinopai-mcp two days ago. It's a local MCP server that gives any AI agent access to crypto intelligence — preflight checks, trade signals, risk state — for USDC micropayments on Base.
What I didn't expect was how much the payment layer would teach me about where agent commerce is actually heading.
If you're building agents in 2026, you're suddenly dealing with a protocol stack that didn't exist 12 months ago:
MCP — how your agent talks to tools
A2A — how agents talk to each other
x402 — how agents pay each other
ACP / UCP / AP2 — how agents pay merchants



That's four layers, three competing standards, and zero consensus on which one to use when.
x402 is cleverly simple: HTTP 402 response → payment header → USDC on Base → retry with receipt. Round-trip under 2 seconds. Fees und…
articles.title: I Built a Pay-Per-Call MCP Server — Here's What the Agent Payment Stack Actually Looks Like

articles.author: Mordecai
articles.description:
A beginner-friendly guide to Docker networking
When you run an application in Docker, it doesn't automatically know how to reach other services. A container is isolated by default — it has its own network namespace, its own IP address, and its own view of the world. For two services to talk, you have to explicitly connect them.
This is something I learned while building SwiftDeploy. My Go API and Nginx were in separate containers and I didn't have full understanding of ow they communicated with each other.
This is the most common scenario — an API and a database, or a frontend and a backend.
The wrong way is to use localhost. If your API tries to connect to localhost:5432 for PostgreSQL, it won't work. Inside a container, localhost refers to the container itself — not your host machine, no…
articles.title: Understanding How Containers Communicate in Docker and Kubernetes

articles.author: airay
articles.description:
I've been experimenting with Chinese LLMs recently and the pricing caught me off guard:



Model
Input (per 1M tokens)
Output (per 1M tokens)




GPT-4o
$2.50
$10.00


DeepSeek V4
$0.30
$0.50


Qwen3.5-Plus
$0.11
$0.67


Qwen-Long
$0.07
$0.28



That's 8-20x cheaper than GPT-4o depending on the model.
From my experience, the main barriers for non-Chinese developers are:
Payment — Most providers only accept Alipay/WeChat Pay
Documentation — English docs are limited or missing
API compatibility — Each provider has its own format
Trust — Concerns about data handling and compliance
I've been running side-by-side tests. For general tasks (chat, summarization, code assistance), DeepSeek and Qwen hold up surprisingly well. They're not beating GPT-4o on everything, but for the price? Hard to ignore.
For those of you who have tried Chinese LLMs — what was your experience? And for those who haven't, what's holding you back?
Would love to hear different perspectives in the comments.
articles.title: Chinese LLMs Are Ridiculously Cheap — Why Aren't More Developers Using Them?
